one_liner: Two-file ANSI C byte-aligned LZ77 block compressor; about 3x zlib -1 compression speed and 2x decompression, at a worse ratio.
what_it_does: FastLZ compresses and decompresses whole in-memory blocks with three C functions: fastlz_compress_level(level, in, len, out), fastlz_decompress(in, len, out, maxout) and a deprecated fastlz_compress. It is not a zlib drop-in: there is no stream API, no container format, no checksum and no stored original size, so the caller must frame blocks and record sizes itself. Level 1 and level 2 outputs are both read by the same decompressor, which detects the level from the first 3 bits of the block.
how_it_is_fast: It is a greedy single-probe LZ77: a 13-bit multiplicative hash (Knuth constant 2654435769) of the next 3 bytes indexes an 8192-entry table of last positions, and a match is taken whenever the 3 bytes agree, with no chain search or lazy matching. Output is byte-aligned opcodes (literal runs up to 32 bytes, short and long matches with 13-bit offsets) with no entropy coding, so decoding is a branch on the top 3 bits plus memcpy/memmove. On x86-64 and aarch64 it reads 32-bit words directly to compare the first 4 bytes of a match.
when_to_use: You need something several times faster than zlib on compressible blocks (text, logs, raw pixel rows, game assets) and can accept roughly 50% output size versus 36% for zlib -1 on Silesia.
You want a tiny, vendorable codec: two files, ANSI C/C90, MIT, compiles with GCC, Clang, MSVC and TinyCC, including DOS and big-endian targets.
You must read data already written in FastLZ format by existing users such as Godot, HHVM or Apache Traffic Server.
Embedded or exotic toolchains where LZ4 or Snappy are harder to build: CI covers PowerPC, ppc64, s390x, armhf, arm64, MIPS and RISC-V.
when_not_to_use: New designs that only want speed: in the same lzbench 2.4 run LZ4 1.10.0 compresses about 2x faster (550 vs 273 MB/s) and decompresses about 6.5x faster (3832 vs 587 MB/s) at a slightly better ratio (47.60% vs 49.37%).
When ratio matters: zstd -1 or zlib-ng -1 give much smaller output at comparable or better speed.
Streams or very large buffers: the API is block-only with int lengths (under 2 GiB per call) and level 1 sees only an 8 KB window (level 2 about 72 KB), so long-range redundancy is lost.
Already compressed inputs (images, video, archives): the README says it is not intended for them and output can grow past the input size.
Projects that want an actively developed codec: last release 0.5.0 is from 2020-02-02 and the format's level 2 is still marked 'To be written' in the README.

integration.dependencies: none (libc string.h only; FASTLZ_USE_MEMMOVE=0 removes even that)
integration.min_toolchain: ANSI C/C90 compiler; CI uses GCC, Clang, TinyCC and VS 2019
integration.platforms: any; 32/64-bit, little and big endian; tested on amd64, i686, i586 DOS, PowerPC, ppc64(le), s390x, armhf, arm64, MIPS(64)(el), RISC-V
integration.thread_safety: Not documented; the functions keep their hash table on the stack and use no globals, so concurrent calls on separate buffers look safe from the source.

gotchas: Compression contract is easy to violate: input must be at least 16 bytes and the output buffer at least 5% larger than the input and no smaller than 66 bytes; there is no compressBound helper and no bounds checking in the compressor.

Decompression returns 0 on corrupt input or a too-small maxout; it was hardened against corrupted input only in 0.5.0 (2020). The README's 40-line reference decoder has no bounds checks and is explicitly unsafe.
The compressor puts a 32 KB hash table (8192 x uint32) on the stack per call, which matters on small embedded stacks.
On x86-64 and aarch64 flz_readu32 dereferences an unaligned uint32_t pointer, which is undefined behavior in C even though it works on those CPUs.
pick_this_over_siblings_when: Pick FastLZ over LZ4 or Snappy only for compatibility with existing FastLZ data or for a C90/TinyCC-portable two-file drop; LZ4 beats it on every axis in lzbench 2.4, and libslz is a similar-speed choice when gzip/deflate output compatibility is needed.
verified_claims_summary: lzbench 2.4 (gcc 15.2.0, -O3, one thread of an AMD EPYC 9555P at 3.20 GHz, turbo off, silesia.tar): fastlz 0.5.0 -1 compresses at 273 MB/s and decompresses at 587 MB/s with output 49.37% of input, versus zlib 1.3.2 -1 at 89.0 / 297 MB/s and 36.45% (about 3.1x and 2.0x, derived from page data). The FastLZ README's own enwik8 table (159 / 305 MB/s vs zlib -1 50 / 184 MB/s) gives no hardware or compiler.
status_note: Stale: last release 0.5.0 in February 2020 and last commits in 2024 are CI and warning fixes, but it is MIT-licensed, two files and widely deployed, so vendoring it is low-risk.
